title: Numbers & Math
description: JavaScript has one number type (double-precision float). Math.* gives you the calculator; parseInt vs Number gives you the parser.

reference.code:
// One number type — integers and floats live together
Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER;   // 9007199254740991 (2^53 - 1)
0.1 + 0.2;                 // 0.30000000000000004  ← float math

// Rounding
Math.floor(3.7);   // 3  — toward -Infinity
Math.ceil(3.2);    // 4  — toward +Infinity
Math.round(3.5);   // 4  — half rounds toward +Infinity
Math.abs(-7);      // 7

// Min / max — pair with spread to work on arrays
Math.max(1, 5, 3);          // 5
Math.max(...[1, 5, 3]);     // 5
Math.min(...[1, 5, 3]);     // 1

// Parsing strings to numbers
Number("42");      // 42
Number("42px");    // NaN          ← strict
parseInt("42px");  // 42           ← lenient, stops at first non-digit
parseInt("ff", 16);// 255          ← always pass the radix
Number.isNaN(NaN); // true
notes: Math.max() with NO arguments returns -Infinity; Math.min() returns +Infinity. Spread an array in to compare its values.
parseInt is lenient ("42px" → 42); Number is strict ("42px" → NaN). Pick by intent.
Floats lose precision: 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3. For money, work in integer cents.

questions.q: What does `Math.max()` return when called with NO arguments?
questions.explain: Surprise: Math.max() returns -Infinity, Math.min() returns +Infinity. Useful as initial accumulators.

questions.q: How do you get the max of an array `nums`?
questions.explain: Math.max takes individual args, so spread the array. `Math.max(nums)` coerces the array to NaN.
Number() is strict; parseInt("42px") would return 42.
IEEE-754 doubles cannot represent 0.1 or 0.2 exactly; the sum is 0.30000000000000004.

exercises.prompt: Find the max and min of an array using spread.

L3.prompt: Write `avg(arr)` that returns the rounded mean of an array. Log `avg([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])`.
hints: Reduce to sum, then divide by length.
